name: Plutonium
occurrence: Found only in extremely trace amounts naturally; almost entirely produced artificially in nuclear reactors from uranium-238.
majorUses: Nuclear weapons (the core material of the 'Fat Man' bomb dropped on Nagasaki)
Radioisotope power sources for deep-space probes (plutonium-238, e.g. Voyager, Curiosity rover)
safetyNotes: Extremely radiotoxic if inhaled or ingested, and its role in nuclear weapons makes it one of the most tightly controlled substances on Earth under international treaties.
notableCharacteristics: Named after Pluto, continuing the pattern from Uranus and Neptune, even though Pluto was later reclassified as a dwarf planet — plutonium's name and classification never changed alongside it.
ncertRelevance: power source for deep space missions
whyHere: Plutonium-239's nucleus, like uranium-235's, is unstable enough to split readily under neutron bombardment, but it's produced rather than mined — created inside reactors when uranium-238 absorbs a neutron and decays, which is exactly why it became central to both nuclear weapons and nuclear power programmes.
didYouKnow: NASA's Voyager 1 and 2 probes, launched in 1977 and still transmitting data from interstellar space, are powered by the slow radioactive decay heat of plutonium-238 — the same element type once made purely for weapons now quietly powers humanity's most distant machines.
genZNote: Powers both nuclear bombs and the Voyager probes still phoning home from interstellar space. Wildest range of any element on this list.
